## Introduction {#sec-introduction}

The political fabric of European democracies has come under sustained strain over the past two decades. Partisan competition has acquired an increasingly affective character, in which citizens not only disagree with the supporters of other parties but actively dislike and distrust them [@iyengar2012affect; @iyengar2019origins; @wagner2021affective; @reiljan2020fear]. At the same time, the cultural and religious composition of European societies has become a focal point of political contestation, with anti-Muslim sentiment emerging as one of the most politically consequential intergroup divisions on the continent [@helbling2014opposing; @arzheimer2018explaining]. These two phenomena, affective polarization and anti-Muslim bias, are usually studied in separate literatures, yet they are entangled in practice. Populist radical right parties (PRRPs) explicitly mobilize anti-Muslim cues to consolidate partisan identities, and citizens process partisan and religious categories simultaneously when they evaluate others.

In this dissertation I take intergroup relations in contemporary European democracies as my overarching topic and ask how partisan and religious group boundaries jointly structure citizens' affective and behavioral responses to one another. My motivation is both substantive and methodological. Substantively, the rise of affective polarization and the growing salience of Muslim identity as a political category rank among the most consequential challenges to liberal democratic cohesion in Europe, and understanding how they interact is essential for assessing the depth of contemporary democratic strain. Methodologically, the comparative study of affective polarization in multiparty systems remains under-specified. Measurement choices about who counts as a partisan, about whether attitudes or behavior is the appropriate outcome, and about how non-partisans should be treated all carry consequences that the existing literature has not systematically resolved [@rollicke2023polarisation; @wagner2024affectiveeurope; @TorcalComellas2025Operationalizing].

I organize the dissertation into three interlocking papers, each of which addresses a different facet of the same underlying question, namely how intergroup boundaries structure political affect and behavior. The three papers share a common empirical foundation and a consistent interest in carefully separating attitudinal from behavioral manifestations of polarization. The empirical core is the cross-national conjoint survey experiment fielded by @hahm2024divided across 25 EU democracies in 2019 (N = 29,800), which combines standard survey items on attachment, ideology, and vote choice with behavioral allocation games (trust and dictator) embedded in randomized conjoint profiles. Because the profiles independently randomize partisan, religious, and demographic attributes, the design supports causal identification of how each attribute shapes intergroup behavior, while the survey component provides the attitudinal counterpart.

The remainder of this proposal proceeds as follows. @sec-redline sets out the conceptual red line connecting the three papers. @sec-data introduces the shared empirical foundation and the paper-specific data extensions I plan to pursue. @sec-csap through @sec-hmr then present each paper in turn, focusing on the research question, the prior literature, the analytical strategy at the level of logic rather than detailed methods, and the contribution to the larger argument. @sec-conclusion closes by drawing the three threads back together and outlining the next steps.

## Red Line: Three Cuts Through One Problem {#sec-redline}

The three papers can be understood as three cuts through the same underlying problem, namely how partisan and religious group categories shape intergroup affect and behavior in Europe, taken at progressively wider analytical scales.

The first cut is the most narrowly methodological. *How* affective polarization is measured determines what conclusions follow about its prevalence and political implications. The choice of who counts as a partisan (self-reported identifiers, vote-anchored partisans, or some combination) and the choice of outcome (party-directed attitudes versus citizen-directed behavior) are not innocuous. In the first paper (CSAP)[^1] I examine this directly and ask whether subjective partisan attachment amplifies polarization beyond what vote-anchored partisanship alone produces. My central empirical contribution there is to separate vertical AP (attitudes toward parties) from horizontal AP (behavior toward fellow citizens) and to compare explicit and implicit partisans on both dimensions.

[^1]: Throughout this proposal I refer to the three planned papers by internal project abbreviations, as final titles have not yet been settled: CSAP (Comparative Study of Affective Polarization), MAP (Muslimhood × Affective Polarization), and HMR (Historical Muslim Rule).

The second cut introduces a second group dimension. Once partisan AP has been characterized, the question becomes how it interacts with other salient identity divides, a question central to the social sorting literature. In the second paper (MAP) I take up the religious dimension specifically and ask how anti-Muslim bias interacts with partisan affect. The conjoint design's orthogonal randomization of partisanship and religion makes this interaction directly estimable, and an exploratory finding from the same data motivates the paper, namely that copartisans are penalized *more* heavily when presented as Muslim than outpartisans are. This asymmetry suggests that religious identity does not simply add to partisan affect but reshapes its internal structure, weakening in-group favoritism more than it amplifies out-group derogation.

The third cut moves from the contemporary cross-section to the long-run structural context in which present-day attitudes are formed. In the third paper (HMR) I ask whether the historical legacy of Muslim rule in parts of Europe shapes contemporary anti-Muslim bias and support for far-right parties, and I develop a probabilistic framework for treating the resulting treatment variable with the uncertainty it warrants. This paper provides a macro-historical complement to the micro-individual analysis of MAP. Where MAP estimates how Muslim identity interacts with partisanship in citizens' present-day allocations, HMR asks whether the underlying baseline of anti-Muslim bias is itself shaped by deep historical exposure to Muslim governance.

The three papers thus form a sequence of progressively wider explanatory scales: from measurement of the partisan divide (CSAP), to its interaction with a cross-cutting group dimension (MAP), to the historical-structural conditions shaping that group dimension's contemporary expression (HMR). They are tied together by a single primary dataset, by a consistent commitment to distinguishing attitudinal from behavioral outcomes, and by a shared analytical concern with how group boundaries, whether partisan, religious, or historical, jointly structure intergroup relations in contemporary Europe.

@tbl-overview summarizes the structure.

| Paper | Scale | Group divide(s) | Outcome focus | Identification strategy |
|:------|:------|:----------------|:--------------|:------------------------|
| CSAP | Micro / measurement | Partisanship (explicit vs. implicit) | Vertical (thermometer) + horizontal (game allocation) | Within-party comparison; Bayesian multilevel |
| MAP  | Micro / interactive | Partisanship × religion (Muslim) | Behavioral allocation | Conjoint AMCEs; reweighting to realistic joint distribution |
| HMR  | Macro / structural | Historical Muslim rule × contemporary Muslim bias / PRRP vote | Behavioral allocation + vote choice | Spatial multilevel; probabilistic treatment surface |

## Data {#sec-data}

My main primary data source across all three papers is the cross-national conjoint survey experiment fielded by @hahm2024divided in 2019 (the EU25 data, N $\approx$ 29,800). The survey was administered online to roughly 1,200 respondents in each of 25 European democracies, covering the EU member states at the time of data collection, including the United Kingdom, with the exception of Luxembourg, Malta, and Cyprus. Each respondent completed standard demographic and attitudinal batteries, including feeling-thermometer ratings of the major parties and a partisan-attachment item, reported vote choice and vote intention, and a set of behavioral allocation games (dictator and trust) in which they distributed tokens to randomized conjoint profiles. The profiles independently randomize partisan, religious, and demographic attributes, so the design isolates the causal effect of each attribute on intergroup behavior [@hainmueller2014causal].

This dataset is well suited to my research program for two reasons. First, it carries both instruments that the affective-polarization literature relies on. It includes the traditional feeling-thermometer scales used to measure attitudinal polarization and the conjoint behavioral games used to measure discriminatory behavior. Because both instruments are answered by the **same respondents** under a **consistent research design across 25 countries**, the data allow a comprehensive cross-national comparison of attitudinal (thermometer-based) and behavioral (game-based) affective polarization that is difficult to assemble from separate national surveys. Second, the conjoint component independently randomizes religion alongside partisanship, which makes the partisan-by-religion interaction at the center of MAP directly estimable, and it geolocates respondents, which makes the linkage to historical contact zones at the center of HMR feasible.

The major limitation is temporal. The data were collected in 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic, and are therefore likely outdated relative to the current configuration of European party systems and intergroup attitudes. I intend to incorporate additional external data sources to improve validity and to extend the analysis beyond a single pre-pandemic cross-section. I state transparently that, for two of the three papers, these external sources are not yet in place, and I treat their current absence as an honest limitation rather than a solved problem. Each paper draws on a different strength of the EU25 data and faces a distinct data limitation, which I set out in the relevant paper sections below.

## Paper 1 (CSAP): Does Partisan Attachment Amplify Affective Polarization? {#sec-csap}

### Question and motivation

In the first paper I ask a simple but consequential measurement question: does self-reported partisan attachment amplify affective polarization beyond what vote-anchored partisanship alone produces, and does the answer depend on whether the outcome is party-directed attitudes or citizen-directed behavior?

My motivation is that the comparative AP literature has not resolved this question. Studies using the @reiljan2020fear index typically condition on self-reported identifiers, whereas studies using the @wagner2021affective spread measure include the full electorate. The choice matters more in multiparty Europe than in the United States, because the share of citizens who report attachment varies dramatically across European countries, ranging in my data from roughly 40% in Latvia to over 80% in Denmark. Restricting the sample to explicit identifiers therefore changes the population of inference differently in each national context, and the substantive comparability of cross-national AP estimates depends on whether the omitted group, namely voters who deny attachment but reveal a partisan anchor through vote choice, polarizes in the same way as those who do report attachment.

### Theory and prior literature

The contemporary study of polarization shifted attention from ideological distance toward affective orientations once scholars recognized that partisan conflict is driven by social and emotional divisions as much as by policy disagreement [@iyengar2012affect; @fiorina2008polarization; @poole1984polarization; @mccarty2006polarized]. Rooted in social identity and self-categorization theory, affective polarization is now defined as the tendency to feel warmth toward partisan in-groups and hostility toward out-groups [@iyengar2015fear; @iyengar2019origins; @tajfel1971social; @Sherif1961intergroup; @brewer1999psychology]. A large comparative literature documents its prevalence well beyond the United States, across European multiparty systems [@wagner2021affective; @reiljan2020fear; @boxell2024cross]. As the field has matured, the cumulative task has shifted from establishing whether AP exists toward clarifying what precisely is being measured and for whom theoretical claims hold [@campos2025new; @IyengarWagner2025Conceptualizing; @CarlinLove2025Measuring].

Two refinements are central to my design. First, scholars distinguish vertical AP, directed at parties and elites, from horizontal AP, directed at fellow citizens [@druckman2019we; @areal2024verticalvshorizontal; @klar2018affective]. Second, they distinguish attitudinal measures such as feeling thermometers from behavioral measures such as allocation decisions in economic games [@CarlinLove2025Measuring; @iyengar2015fear]. These dimensions need not coincide. Citizens may express dislike without discriminating behaviorally, or discriminate without reporting hostility, so conflating elite-directed attitudes with citizen-directed behavior risks obscuring distinct underlying mechanisms.

The question of who counts as a partisan implicates competing accounts of AP's psychological foundations. Social-identity accounts treat subjective attachment as the bond that intensifies affective investment, predicting that explicit identifiers polarize more strongly than voters who merely reveal a partisan anchor through vote choice [@huddy2015expressive; @mason2018one]. Categorization and cue-processing accounts hold that partisan labels and vote anchors are sufficient to generate polarized responses even absent felt attachment [@orr2023affective; @orr2020policy; @dafoe2018information]. This contrast extends classic work on independents, leaners, and implicit partisanship [@petrocik2009measuring; @kinder2017neither; @theodoridis2017me; @elliott2024like] to the multiparty setting, where the stakes are higher because the share of explicit identifiers varies sharply across countries and reshapes the population of inference differently in each [@rollicke2023polarisation; @TorcalComellas2025Operationalizing; @garzia2023affective]. By comparing explicit and implicit partisans on both the vertical and the horizontal dimension, I adjudicate between these accounts while clarifying the sampling decisions on which cross-national AP estimates depend.

### Conceptual move

I distinguish two partisan types. *Explicit* partisans report feeling attached to a party, and *implicit* partisans deny attachment but reveal a partisan anchor through reported vote intention or recall. This terminology serves primarily as a consistent analytical category for cross-national comparison rather than as a novel theoretical construct. As set out above, it nevertheless provides leverage on whether social-identity or categorization accounts better describe the data. Identity accounts predict that explicit partisans are more polarized than implicit partisans, whereas categorization accounts predict equivalence.

My second conceptual step separates vertical from horizontal AP. I measure vertical AP through thermometer ratings of parties, which capture attitudes toward parties as collective political objects, and I measure horizontal AP through behavioral allocations in conjoint trust and dictator games, which capture discriminatory behavior toward fellow citizens. The two are often conflated in the literature but may track different psychological mechanisms [@druckman2019we; @areal2024verticalvshorizontal; @CarlinLove2025Measuring]. Testing partisan-type differences on both dimensions separately is the central empirical contribution of the paper.

### Preliminary finding and identification

My exploratory analyses on the EU25 data show a clear asymmetry. Explicit partisans display systematically higher vertical AP than implicit partisans across all 25 countries, but the two groups are indistinguishable on horizontal behavioral discrimination. If this pattern holds under more rigorous analysis, it implies that subjective attachment shapes party-directed *attitudes* but not citizen-directed *behavior*, a finding that challenges unified theories of AP and carries direct implications for measurement practice.

The most pressing inferential concern is selection. Explicit and implicit partisans differ systematically in ideological extremity, political interest, and related traits, so a naive comparison conflates the effect of expressed attachment with the effect of the underlying traits that produce it. My strategy is to restrict the comparison to parties that contain *both* explicit and implicit partisans in non-trivial numbers and to estimate within-party effects, complemented by propensity-score balancing on observed covariates. This converts the estimand from "do identifiers polarize more on average?" to "within the same party, does declaring attachment raise AP?", which is a narrower but more defensible causal claim. I estimate these models using Bayesian multilevel specifications with country-level random effects, which account for the nested structure and yield posterior distributions that make uncertainty propagation through the analysis straightforward.

### Data: strengths and extensions

For this paper the central strength of the EU25 data is that the same respondents provide both the thermometer ratings that define vertical AP and the conjoint game allocations that define horizontal AP, which is precisely what makes a like-for-like comparison of the two dimensions possible within a single sample and design. The principal limitation is the single 2019 cross-section. To improve validity and to test whether the vertical-horizontal asymmetry generalizes beyond these data, I plan to draw on existing affective-polarization trust-game data from other time points and countries, most notably the behavioral games in @Westwood2018tie, and on widely used thermometer-based AP datasets such as the American National Election Studies (ANES) and the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES). <!-- TODO: missing bib entries for the ANES and CSES datasets -->

### Contribution

My contribution is twofold. Substantively, the paper provides the first systematic test, in comparative perspective, of whether subjective attachment amplifies AP equally on the attitudinal and the behavioral dimension. Methodologically, it offers guidance on sampling decisions for comparative AP research. If the vertical-horizontal asymmetry holds, then combining explicit and implicit partisans is defensible when the outcome is behavioral but not when it is attitudinal.

## Paper 2 (MAP): Partisan Sorting and the Muslim Penalty {#sec-map}

### Question and motivation

In the second paper I take the partisan AP characterized in CSAP as given and ask how it interacts with anti-Muslim bias, the most politically salient non-partisan group divide in contemporary Europe. The motivating observation, drawn from preliminary work on the same dataset, is that copartisans are penalized *more* in token allocations when they are presented as Muslim than outpartisans are. The negative effect of Muslim identity on trust-game allocations is larger when applied to copartisans than to outpartisans. This is theoretically puzzling. If Muslim identity simply added a fixed penalty across the board, partisan AP would be preserved. If it amplified out-group derogation more than it suppressed in-group favoritism, AP would intensify. What the data appear to show is the opposite. Muslim identity suppresses copartisan favoritism more strongly than it amplifies out-partisan derogation, with the net effect of *reducing* the partisan affective gap when the target is Muslim.

### Theory and prior literature

I situate this puzzle in the literature on *social sorting*, which argues that affective polarization intensifies when multiple social identities, whether partisan, religious, ethnic, or regional, align along the same political fault line. The alignment of these identities produces what @mason2018one calls "mega-identities" that sharpen the in-group and out-group boundary and deepen partisan affect [@mason2015disrespectfully; @mason2018ideologues; @mason2016acrosscutting; @mason2013therise]. The complementary expectation from cross-cutting cleavage theory is that identities pulling in different directions moderate polarization, because they complicate the boundaries of political conflict and make disagreement less likely to be experienced as existential [@roccas2002social; @gaertner1993common; @gaertner2000reducing; @levendusky2018americans].

Although this work originated in the two-party context of the United States, its logic travels to Europe, where sorting operates along the historically embedded cleavages of class, religion, and region and increasingly intersects with newer conflicts over immigration and European integration [@harteveld2021ticking; @lipset1967partysystem; @Hooghe2018cleavage; @Kriesi2006globalization]. Most comparative work in this tradition, however, has focused on the *level* of partisan AP under different patterns of sorting [@gidron2020american; @hahm2023dividedby]. I take a different cut. Rather than asking whether sorting raises or lowers AP overall, I ask how the *internal structure* of partisan affect, that is the relative weight of in-group favoritism versus out-group derogation, is reshaped when partisan and religious identities are crossed at the level of the individual evaluation. This directional and asymmetric question is what the focus on aggregate AP levels has tended to obscure.

### Conceptual move

Standard treatments of cross-cutting identities predict that, when a salient out-group attribute (Muslim, from the perspective of European majorities) is orthogonally distributed across partisan affiliations, affective polarization should be *moderated*, because the in-group and out-group boundary becomes harder to draw. My finding complicates this prediction. The moderation does not happen symmetrically. It does not produce a uniform softening of partisan affect. Instead it produces a strong, targeted penalty on copartisan Muslims that approaches or exceeds the size of partisan AP itself. My conceptual contribution is to argue that social sorting and cross-cutting identities can reshape AP asymmetrically, weakening in-group favoritism more than out-group derogation, and that this asymmetry, rather than the aggregate level of AP, is what the sorting literature has been missing.

### Identification and the external-validity extension

The empirical core of the paper is an external-validity extension of the conjoint analysis that the existing literature on partisan-religious sorting has not yet implemented. By design, the conjoint assigns Muslim identity uniformly across partisan profiles. This is internally valid and makes the interaction directly estimable, but it is externally unrealistic in a way that matters for the substantive interpretation. Muslim voters are concentrated in particular parties, namely centre-left and ethnic minority parties, and are nearly absent from the support base of radical right parties. The uniform assignment therefore inflates the empirical frequency of combinations, such as a Muslim radical-right copartisan, that essentially do not occur in the electorate. Conventional AMCE estimates aggregated across this uniform distribution thus describe a population that does not exist.

To address this, I extend the standard AMCE framework using the population-weighted estimator developed by @de2022improving, which aligns the conjoint estimand with the empirical joint distribution of profile attributes in the target population. Concretely, I reweight the AMCEs to the country-specific empirical joint distribution of partisanship and religion, so that the estimated effect of Muslim identity on allocations reflects the combinations of partisanship and religion that voters actually encounter in their political environment. This extension is the methodological centerpiece of the paper. It allows a direct test of whether the asymmetric copartisan penalty is a substantive feature of how Europeans process partisan-religious co-identities or, in part, an artifact of the experimental design's uniform attribute distribution.

### Data: strengths and extensions

The strength of the EU25 data for this paper lies in its design. The conjoint independently and orthogonally randomizes religion alongside partisanship, which is what makes the partisan-by-religion interaction estimable in the first place and what creates the experimental condition of cross-cuttingness on which the analysis rests. Two limitations are nonetheless serious. First, I would like to corroborate the experimental result with additional data, but given the specific setup, namely the interaction of the partisan AP divide with anti-Muslim discrimination, I have not yet identified a suitable external source that pairs a comparable behavioral measure with sufficient variation in both dimensions. I treat this as a crucial current limitation of the paper. Second, the token-allocation outcome is bounded, and allocations to stigmatized Muslim profiles cluster near the bottom of the scale, which raises the risk of ceiling (more precisely, floor) effects that could mechanically compress or distort the estimated interaction. I will address this risk explicitly in the modeling strategy, for example through specifications that respect the bounded outcome and through sensitivity analyses, so that the asymmetric copartisan penalty cannot be dismissed as a mechanical artifact of the measurement scale.

### Contribution

The paper contributes to two literatures. First, it speaks to the social sorting and affective polarization literatures by demonstrating that the interaction of partisanship with other salient identity divides can reshape the internal structure of partisan affect asymmetrically, a finding that the existing focus on aggregate AP levels has obscured. Second, it speaks to the literature on anti-Muslim bias by showing that the penalty associated with Muslim identity is not uniform but is conditioned on partisan alignment, and is in fact *stronger* among ostensibly aligned copartisan co-players than among out-partisans. My use of the @de2022improving framework to recover externally valid estimates is itself a methodological contribution to the comparative conjoint literature, which to date has largely relied on uniformly distributed designs.

## Paper 3 (HMR): Historical Muslim Rule and Contemporary Anti-Muslim Bias {#sec-hmr}

### Question and core idea

In the third paper I step back from the cross-section and ask whether the contemporary anti-Muslim bias studied in MAP is shaped by deep historical exposure to Muslim governance in parts of Europe. Substantial regions of present-day Spain, Portugal, southern Italy, parts of the Balkans, Hungary, and elsewhere experienced extended periods of Muslim rule. The most prominent cases are Al-Andalus (711 to 1492) and Ottoman Europe (fourteenth to early twentieth century), but smaller and shorter-lived polities also governed Sicily, Malta, Provence (Fraxinetum), and the southern Italian mainland. I ask whether this historical exposure leaves cultural traces that shape contemporary anti-Muslim bias and, through it, support for populist radical right parties (PRRPs).

My conceptual frame is the *Behavioral Theory of Culture* (BToC) that I develop as part of this research program. BToC defines culture not as a static set of beliefs or values but as an emergent property of repeated, identity-linked behaviors that persist intergenerationally. Under this framing, sustained historical contact between Muslim rulers and non-Muslim populations, under cooperative rather than purely conflictual conditions and over sufficient duration, generated routinized behavioral residues in food, language, architecture, and everyday custom. These residues expand the associative complexity of the category "Muslim" in present-day populations, and that greater complexity should attenuate the rhetorical effectiveness of threat-based PRRP appeals.

### Theory and prior literature

This paper draws together three literatures. The first concerns the nature of anti-Muslim bias in Europe. Although it is often subsumed under generic xenophobia, this bias is bound specifically to perceived religious identity rather than to national origin or skin color, and it is triggered above all by the perception that Muslims are highly and visibly religious [@helbling2014opposing; @helbling2014framing; @bleich2011islamophobia]. PRRPs treat this latent bias as a resource, embedding anti-Muslim appeals in a civilizational narrative that casts Islam as incompatible with European values [@arzheimer2018explaining; @mudde2004populist; @betz1994radical].

The second literature is intergroup contact theory, which holds that contact between groups can reduce prejudice under conditions of cooperation, equal status, and shared goals [@allport_nature_1954; @pettigrew_meta_analytic_2006]. I extend this framework across historical time. Reconceptualizing past episodes of Muslim rule as long-run "contact zones" [@pratt_1991_arts], I argue that sustained historical co-presence can operate analogously to interpersonal contact, leaving behavioral residues that increase familiarity and complicate monolithic stereotypes long after direct memory has faded.

The third literature studies historical legacies and persistence, asking whether deep historical experiences shape present-day political behavior. It has linked, for example, medieval persecution to later anti-Semitic violence and proximity to historical repression to contemporary far-right support [@cirone2022historical; @acharya2024historical; @nunn2020historical; @voigtlander_persecution_2012; @homola_legacies_2020; @haffert_long-term_2022; @oto_peralias_economic_2016; @obschonka2025roma]. This literature also cautions that historical contact need not integrate, because memories of violent rule can heighten rather than reduce symbolic distance [@ochsner_activated_2024]. A recurring methodological critique is that persistence studies tend to treat historical treatments as known when they are in fact estimated [@guinnane_persistence_2022; @moller2026social; @conley2025standard], a concern that directly motivates the uncertainty-aware design I describe below.

### Research design

The design links a georeferenced dataset on historical Muslim rule to the EU25 conjoint and survey data. The conjoint games supply the central outcome. Because each profile randomizes religion independently of its other attributes, the effect of a Muslim profile on token allocation furnishes a *behavioral* measure of anti-Muslim bias, one less exposed to social-desirability pressures than self-reports. I geolocate respondents to regions of historical Muslim rule, coded both as a binary indicator and as the logged duration of rule. The core hypothesis is that anti-Muslim bias is *moderated* by historical contact: the penalty attached to Muslim profiles should be attenuated among respondents in historical contact zones. I estimate this as an interaction between profile religion and respondent contact status, and I extend the same logic to a second outcome, support for PRRPs. Multilevel models with country-level random intercepts accommodate the nesting of respondents within countries.

The design adds four features that go beyond a conventional persistence analysis.

First, I take source-level uncertainty in the historical treatment seriously. Existing approaches to coding historical treatments rely on deterministic polygons drawn from secondary syntheses. The boundaries of polities like Al-Andalus, however, were neither sharp nor stable. Frontier zones were often contested or tributary rather than fully ruled, and the source basis for delineation, which ranges from chronicles and coin finds to toponymic evidence and archaeology, varies enormously in density and reliability across regions and periods. I replace deterministic polygons with a probabilistic raster in which each location-period carries an assigned probability of Muslim rule, with prior uncertainty calibrated to the type and density of available sources. Treatment quantities such as ever-ruled and duration then become expectations over this distribution, and the resulting uncertainty propagates into the second-stage regression. Where the historical record is dense and consistent, the treatment is assigned with high confidence. Where it is thin or contested, the treatment is assigned probabilistically and the resulting uncertainty is carried through to the substantive estimate rather than hidden behind a crisp polygon. This directly addresses the critique that the historical persistence literature tends to treat historical treatments as known when they are in fact estimated [@moller2026social; @conley2025standard].

Second, I operationalize the cultural-trace mechanism empirically. The BToC argument hinges on the persistence of routinized, identity-linked behaviors as the mechanism through which historical contact reduces contemporary bias. To date, evidence for such traces, for instance saffron in Valencian cuisine, Arabic-derived toponyms, or surviving architectural elements, has been anecdotal. I develop a more systematic approach to measuring cultural traces at the regional level. Candidate measures include toponymic density (the share of place names of Arabic or Ottoman-Turkish origin), surviving culinary vocabulary, architectural inventory, and loanword density in regional dialects. Aggregating these into a regional cultural-trace index allows a direct mediation test. I can then ask whether the effect of historical contact on contemporary bias operates through the persistence of cultural traces or instead through some other channel, whether institutional, demographic, or economic, that the design has not isolated. Even partial success here would move the BToC argument from theoretical motivation to testable mechanism.

Third, I measure party-level anti-Muslim mobilization systematically. The link from historical contact to PRRP support is necessarily indirect. It runs through anti-Muslim bias, which in turn matters for voting only insofar as PRRPs actually mobilize against Muslims rhetorically. If radical right parties in a given country or region instead emphasize other issues, such as corruption, EU integration, or economic protection, the bias-reducing effect of historical contact has no rhetorical channel through which to translate into vote choice. I will assemble a systematic measure of party-level anti-Muslim mobilization, drawing on manifesto data, campaign salience measures, and expert codings. Interacting historical contact with mobilization intensity yields a conditional hypothesis, namely that historical contact reduces PRRP support *where and when* PRRPs deploy anti-Muslim appeals as a salient part of their political offer. This extension also connects HMR more tightly to MAP, since both papers then engage with how political mobilization along religious lines structures intergroup behavior.

Fourth, I add administrative electoral data at the NUTS3 level. The EU25 survey is a single cross-section from 2019 and, though comparatively large, has limited statistical power for fine-grained regional analyses, particularly in the smaller historical contact zones. To improve external validity and statistical power on the voting outcome, I supplement the survey-based PRRP vote measure with administrative electoral data at the NUTS3 level, which I have already collected. Regional vote shares for PRRPs across multiple elections allow both a more reliable estimate of the historical-contact effect on PRRP support and an extension of the analysis beyond 2019, which yields at least preliminary descriptive evidence on whether the relationship varies with the salience of immigration and identity politics across electoral cycles. The respondent-level survey analysis remains my primary individual-level identification strategy, and the NUTS3 data provide aggregate-level corroboration on a much larger and more temporally extended outcome base.

### Data: strengths and extensions

For this paper the EU25 data offer three specific advantages. The conjoint games yield the behavioral bias measure described above, the design is cross-national, and respondents are geocoded, which is what makes it possible to link individuals to subnational zones of historical Muslim rule. The corresponding limitation is that the survey is a single 2019 cross-section with modest power in the smaller contact zones. Beyond the NUTS3 electoral data discussed above, I am therefore considering external projects such as the World Values Survey for measures that capture anti-Muslim bias and are available at least at a regional, subnational level, which would let me test the persistence of historical effects on a broader and more temporally varied basis. <!-- TODO: missing bib entry for the World Values Survey -->

### Contribution

The paper contributes to three literatures. To the historical persistence literature it offers a treatment assignment that takes source-level uncertainty seriously and a more systematic operationalization of the cultural mechanism through which legacies are theorized to persist. To the contact theory literature it extends the framework across deep historical time, asking whether sustained historical co-presence operates analogously to interpersonal contact in shaping intergroup cognition. To the PRRP literature it tests whether the link from anti-Muslim bias to far-right support is conditional on the rhetorical strategies that parties actually deploy, a conditionality that comparative work on PRRP success has largely treated as background rather than as a moderator.

## Conclusion and Outlook {#sec-conclusion}

Taken together, the three papers advance an argument that the affective and behavioral fabric of European intergroup relations is structured at three nested scales. At the *measurement* scale, the partisan divide is itself expressed differently depending on whether one looks at attitudes or behavior and on whether one restricts the population to explicit identifiers or includes vote-anchored partisans. These choices have systematic consequences for the substantive picture of polarization that emerges (CSAP). At the *interactive* scale, partisan affect does not operate in isolation but is reshaped by the co-occurrence of other salient identity categories. In the case of Muslim identity, this reshaping may be asymmetric, suppressing in-group favoritism more than it amplifies out-group derogation (MAP). At the *structural-historical* scale, the contemporary baseline of anti-Muslim bias on which all of this rests is itself patterned in part by deep historical exposure to Muslim governance, and the political consequences of that baseline depend on whether radical right parties actually mobilize against Muslims rhetorically (HMR).

The unifying empirical thread is the @hahm2024divided EU25 dataset, which makes the three papers feasible as a coordinated program. The same respondents who provide thermometer-based vertical AP estimates also produce behavioral allocations in the conjoint games, the same conjoint design that supports CSAP's horizontal AP measure also identifies MAP's partisan-religion interaction, and the geolocated respondent base supports HMR's linkage to historical contact zones. Re-preparing this dataset from scratch is my immediate next step and a precondition for all three papers.

Several pieces of the program remain open. The CSAP literature-analysis pipeline, a large-scale review of how the comparative AP literature has handled the in-group selection question, is designed but not yet executed, and I will run it before I finalize the CSAP draft. For MAP, I still need to pin down the estimand formally, choosing among an AMCE interaction, a conditional AMCE, and a heterogeneous treatment effect, and I need to assemble the country-specific partisan-religion joint distributions required for the @de2022improving reweighting step. The four HMR extensions, namely uncertainty-aware treatment assignment, empirical operationalization of cultural traces, systematic party-rhetoric measurement, and NUTS3 administrative electoral data, each require a dedicated data-collection or modeling step before I integrate them into the empirical analysis. Securing the external data sources discussed for each paper remains an open task that I treat honestly as a current limitation of the program.

My broader ambition is that, taken together, the three papers contribute a coherent comparative account of how partisan and religious group boundaries jointly shape intergroup affect and behavior in contemporary European democracies. It is an account that takes measurement seriously, that resists treating individual identity divides in isolation, and that locates contemporary patterns within the historical structures that produced them.
